title: Teaching Quality Through Exemplars
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that expecting quality is not the same as getting it, and that the most effective way to close the gap is to show team members an exemplar of excellent work and discuss why it excels. It observes that people arrive with widely varying experiences and standards, so even strong performers are unlikely to share the leader's standard by default. Presenting a chosen exemplar is the first step; the necessary second step is a conversation that makes the reasons for its excellence explicit. The author urges leaders to collect exemplars for every deliverable they expect, from emails and decks to proposals and spreadsheets, and notes video for physical skills. Knowing what excellence looks like and discussing its nuances, the piece concludes, accelerates learning and skill.
points: Team members bring different standards to their work, so the odds that even top performers match the leader's standard unaided are low.
An exemplar only works when paired with a discussion of why it represents excellence; presenting it is just the first step.
Leaders should be able to point to an exemplar for every deliverable they expect, from white papers and emails to models, timelines and spreadsheets.
Collecting and sharing exemplars goes beyond setting a personal example by giving others an immediate, concrete understanding of what counts as excellent.
quotes: Instead, the best leaders offer team members an exemplar of what excellent looks like. They then discuss why this example shines so brightly. Exemplars are game-changers for talented colleagues.

Team members come to their roles with a wide variety of experiences, expectations, and standards. The odds that they will apply a standard similar to the leader’s regarding the work product is low even for the best performers.

Good leaders narrow those odds by selecting an exemplar that matches the quality they hold high. Presenting this paragon to a team member or team is the first step. What must follow is a discussion that highlights why this example represents the excellence leaders are looking for.

Leaders should be able to point to one or more exemplars for whatever deliverable they expect others to produce. White papers, emails, presentation decks, proposals, models, process maps, project deliverables, speeches, timelines, spreadsheets, and other work products all require something worth emulating if team members are expected to create them with quality.

For more intellectual endeavors, exemplars are usually physical examples of excellent work products produced at an earlier time. From sports to dentistry and from dance movements to lab measurements, the best leaders make it a point to collect exemplars for teaching others.

When team members know what excellence looks like and can discuss the nuances with their leader, learning and skill accelerates. Leaders naturally know how to set an example for others. But by collecting and sharing exemplars, they infuse an immediate understanding of what counts as excellence from which others can learn.
